Gloat

/gloht/ — rhymes with float · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To gloat is to show smug, excessive pride or satisfaction about your own success or someone else's failure, in a way that irritates others.

After winning the bet, Tom couldn't resist gloating about it all week.

Worked Example

At the chess tournament, the young grandmaster stood over his defeated opponent, smirking and narrating every brilliant move he'd made, making sure everyone in the room heard.

Gloat captures not just satisfaction but the SMUG, IRRITATING quality of rubbing it in. Simple 'satisfaction' wouldn't convey the annoying self-satisfaction and the showing-off of it.

How Gloat Sits Among Its Neighbors

Antonyms

humility

modesty

modesty: downplaying your achievements instead of parading them

How Strong Is It? — contentment → pride → smugness → gloat

contentment vs. gloat

contentment vs. gloat: Contentment is the mildest feeling on this scale: quiet satisfaction kept to yourself, nothing like the showy, in-your-face delight of someone who gloats.

pride vs. gloat

pride vs. gloat: Pride is stronger than contentment but still tamer than gloating — pride glows inwardly at a success, while to gloat is to rub that success in everyone's face.

smugness vs. gloat

smugness vs. gloat: Smugness is self-satisfied and annoying, but to gloat is worse: smugness smirks quietly, while gloating openly parades a victory just to irritate the loser.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — gloat (glotta)

Root — gloat (glotta): to grin scornfully, look with sly satisfaction (Old Norse (probable))

Put it together

Put it together: Gloat is a single old root, probably from Old Norse glotta, 'to grin scornfully' — that sly, mocking grin is still the heart of the word: smug, irritating satisfaction at your own win or someone else's failure.

Use the root in a new word: gloating

Use the root in a new word: gloating: Nobody wanted to sit near the gloating champion, whose smug, scornful grin — the original meaning of the old Norse root — never left his face.

Word Building

Word Choice

informal

Gloat is too pointed and mean-spirited for polite company — it's the word for sneering satisfaction, especially when you're happy about someone else's troubles. For simple personal pleasure, just say 'pleased' or 'proud.'
